questions.stem: Wesley, 3, is going home after his viral-induced wheeze has settled. He has his own salbutamol puffer, a spacer and a mask. His mother Kate says she has only ever sprayed her daughter's puffer straight into his mouth. You are showing her how to use the spacer. Which instruction is correct?
options: Fire all the puffs into the spacer, then let him breathe through the mask for a minute
Fire one puff, then ask him to take one deep breath and hold it for 10 seconds
Shake before each puff, seal the mask, fire one puff, then let him take 4 normal breaths
Fire one puff, then take the mask off as soon as he has taken a single breath
questions.why: In a preschool child the mask must seal over the nose and mouth. Shake the puffer, fire one puff at a time and let him take about 4 normal (tidal) breaths after each puff, then repeat until the full dose is given.
notes: Firing several puffs into the spacer at once makes the aerosol stick together and settle on the spacer wall, so much less of the drug is inhaled.
A deep breath and a 10-second breath-hold is the mouthpiece technique for older children; a 3-year-old cannot do it reliably, so tidal breathing through a mask is used.
One breath does not clear the spacer, so much of each puff is lost; about 4 tidal breaths are needed for each puff.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, 15 kg, is in ED with viral-induced wheeze. Twenty minutes after his first dose of salbutamol (6 puffs by spacer and mask) he has RR 40, SpO2 95% on room air and HR 156. He is alert, with mild subcostal recession and an ongoing wheeze. The registrar is in resus. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat salbutamol 6 puffs by spacer and mask, reassessing 20 minutes after each dose
Add ipratropium 4 puffs by spacer to the next salbutamol dose and repeat each 20 minutes
Give oral prednisolone 15 mg now and continue salbutamol every 3 hours on the ward
Start nasal prong oxygen to keep SpO2 at 96% or above, then repeat the salbutamol dose
questions.why: In a moderate episode that is improving, the first-line treatment is salbutamol 6 puffs by spacer (dose for under 6 years), repeated every 20 minutes for up to 3 doses in the first hour, with a reassessment after each dose. Then space the doses out as he responds.
notes: Ipratropium is added in the first hour only for a severe episode or a poor response to salbutamol. Wesley has a moderate episode and is improving.
Oral prednisolone isn't routine in preschool viral wheeze. It is reserved for severe episodes, a poor response or admission. Wesley isn't stable on 3-hourly salbutamol yet.
Oxygen is only needed if SpO2 falls below 92%, and then the aim is to keep it at 92% or above. At 95% on room air, Wesley doesn't need oxygen.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, has had a cold for 2 days and now makes a high-pitched whistling noise mainly when he breathes out. You hear bilateral wheeze on auscultation. His mother asks why the noise comes on the out-breath rather than the in-breath. Which mechanism best explains an expiratory wheeze?
options: Extrathoracic airways collapse as pressure inside them falls below atmospheric pressure
Airway smooth muscle contracts only during expiration, narrowing the bronchi each breath
Fluid and exudate in the alveoli pop open and shut at the end of each expiration
Rising pleural pressure in expiration compresses narrowed intrathoracic airways further
questions.why: During expiration, pleural pressure rises and squeezes the intrathoracic airways, which are already narrowed by viral inflammation. Air moving fast through these narrowed airways makes the walls oscillate, which produces the wheeze. A child's small airways make this worse.
notes: This describes extrathoracic (upper) airway collapse during inspiration, which causes inspiratory stridor, as in croup. It doesn't cause an expiratory wheeze.
Bronchospasm doesn't switch on and off with each breath. It is sustained, and it is the changing pleural pressure that makes the narrowing worse in expiration.
Alveolar fluid gives crackles, not a musical wheeze, and suggests pneumonia. Wesley has no focal crackles.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, has access to his older sister's Lego. His story fits viral wheeze, but you still ask about a sudden choking episode. If a small Lego piece had passed his larynx, where would it most likely lodge, and why?
options: Left main bronchus, because it is longer and leaves the trachea at a steeper angle
Right main bronchus, because it is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left
Left lower lobe bronchus, because the aortic arch pushes the left bronchus vertical
Right upper lobe bronchus, because it is the first branch and points straight upward
questions.why: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and closer to the line of the trachea than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually go to the right. Suspect one if there was a sudden choking episode or the chest signs are one-sided.
notes: The left main bronchus is longer, but it leaves the trachea at a more horizontal angle because it has to pass under the aortic arch. That makes it the less likely side.
The aortic arch arches over the left main bronchus and makes it run more horizontally, not more vertically. The left bronchial tree is not the usual site.
The right upper lobe bronchus runs upward and outward, against gravity and the direction of airflow. Objects more often lodge in the right main bronchus, bronchus intermedius or lower lobe bronchus.
